meta.title: Who really said "I like your Christ, I do not like your Christians"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No Gandhi source exists. The documented antecedent is a remark by 'Bara Dada' recorded in E. Stanley Jones's The Christ of the Indian Road (1925). The earliest Gandhi attribution is 1927, second-hand, and in a shorter form.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I like your Christ, I do not like your Christians'?
meta.ogDescription: Not sourced to Gandhi. The antecedent is a line by 'Bara Dada' in a 1925 missionary book — and Gandhi's real advice to Christians, from the same book, is more pointed.

answer.label: Not sourced to Gandhi — antecedent is 'Bara Dada'
answer.authorDates: antecedent recorded 1925; first credited to Gandhi 1927
answer.sourceLine: Nothing in the Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi contains this, and no contemporaneous record has it. The documented ancestor is a remark by a man E. Stanley Jones calls “Bara Dada” in The Christ of the Indian Road (1925): “Jesus is ideal and wonderful, but you Christians — you are not like him.” The earliest attribution to Gandhi we can date is 1927, reported second-hand, and shorter: “I like your Christ, but not your Christianity.”

“I like your Christ, but not your Christianity”

source.excerpt: All of you Christians, missionaries and all, must begin to live more like Jesus Christ.
trail: The antecedent is in E. Stanley Jones’s The Christ of the Indian Road (1925), where a man he calls ‘Bara Dada’ — Bengali for ‘eldest brother,’ generally identified as Dwijendranath Tagore, though we flag that as inference — says ‘Jesus is ideal and wonderful, but you Christians — you are not like him’ the book ↗.

The earliest attribution to Gandhi we can date is the Harvard Crimson of 11 January 1927 — and it is hearsay, relayed by a visitor reporting conversations in India, in the shorter form ‘I like your Christ, but not your Christianity.’ The modern three-clause version is a later compression 1927 report ↗.

Gandhi did tell Jones what he thought Christians should do, and it is recorded in the same book: begin by living more like Jesus Christ, practise the faith without adulterating it, emphasise love, and study other religions sympathetically. That is the sourced version of the sentiment Jones on Gandhi ↗.
source.excerptNote: The first of four suggestions Gandhi gave Jones when asked how Christianity might take root in India. Quoted from Jones’s account; we have not inspected the page itself, and flag it as strongly corroborated rather than primary-verified.

Jones’s The Christ of the Indian Road (1925) is in the United States public domain, so both the Bara Dada line and Gandhi’s four suggestions may be quoted freely with credit. author.name: Mahatma Gandhi
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Gandhi
author.metaLine: 1869–1948 · leader of the Indian independence movement
author.bio: Mohandas K. Gandhi (1869–1948) admired Jesus, quoted the Sermon on the Mount throughout his life, and was openly critical of institutional Christianity — which makes this line so plausible that few people think to check it. He is also among the most quote-magnetized figures of the twentieth century: an epigram about hypocrisy and faith attaches to him almost automatically.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-quoted things Gandhi never said — and unusually, the real speaker is recorded, in a book Gandhi himself appears in.

items.tag: no source in the Collected Works
items.why: Nothing in his published writings or speeches contains it, and no contemporaneous record has him saying it. The Collected Works — freely searchable — does not carry it survey of fake Gandhi quotes ↗.
Jones records the remark from a different Indian interlocutor entirely, in simpler words. The polished three-clause epigram we know today is a later tightening of that line onto a more famous name.
A longer version circulates with an appended paragraph about affluent Christian countries contradicting Christ. That tail has no source at all — not Gandhi, not Jones, not Bara Dada.

misattribution.truthLine: Not sourced to Gandhi. The documented antecedent is Bara Dada’s remark in Jones (1925); the earliest Gandhi credit is second-hand, from 1927, and shorter 1927 report ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It lets a Christian audience hear a devastating criticism from someone they admire rather than from an opponent — which is exactly why it is quoted from pulpits as often as against them. The politeness of ‘I like your Christ’ is what makes the second half land.

Gandhi’s actual recorded advice to missionaries is blunter and harder to use as a rhetorical flourish: live more like Jesus, do not water down your faith, put love at the centre, and take other religions seriously enough to find what is good in them.
detailsBody: 1925, Jones records ‘Bara Dada’: ‘Jesus is ideal and wonderful, but you Christians — you are not like him.’
1925, same book, Gandhi’s own advice: ‘All of you Christians, missionaries and all, must begin to live more like Jesus Christ.’
1927, Harvard Crimson, second-hand: ‘I like your Christ, but not your Christianity.’
Later: compressed into the modern three-clause form and credited to Gandhi; sometimes extended with an unsourced paragraph about affluent Christian countries.
context.pull: The real speaker is recorded — in the same book Gandhi appears in.
